title: History and philosophy
note: Modern martial arts carry older ideas. Nitobe's Bushido (1900) presented samurai ethics to Western readers; Musashi's Book of Five Rings distilled strategy; Kano made jujutsu an education; Bruce Lee's Jeet Kune Do prized adaptability; the Gracies turned judo-based jiu-jitsu into ground fighting that reshaped modern MMA.

read.title: Nitobe's Bushido
text: In 1899, Inazo Nitobe, a Japanese scholar living in Malvern, Pennsylvania, finished a short book in English for Western readers. A Belgian professor had asked him how Japanese schools taught morals without religious instruction, and Nitobe's answer was the samurai code he called Bushido, which he rendered literally as Military-Knight-Ways.

Nitobe did not present a written rulebook. He described an unwritten ethic drawn from Buddhism, Shinto, and above all the teachings of Confucius, and he organized it as a set of virtues: rectitude, courage, benevolence, politeness, veracity, honor, loyalty, and self-control. Of rectitude he wrote, "Rectitude is the bone that gives firmness and stature." Courage, for him, was not mere daring; restating a Confucian saying, he concluded, "Courage is doing what is right."

Nitobe also stressed the warrior's mercy, bushi no nasake, the tenderness of a warrior. Historians debate how closely real samurai matched his portrait, and the book is partly an idealized defense of Japan to the West. Still, it shaped how the world, and modern martial artists, came to think about character in training.
